prompt:
Pixel-art sprite sheet, single image, fully transparent background.

SUBJECT: the undead zombie basketball player in the attached reference image.
Match that character exactly: sickly grey-green skin, ragged mid-brown hair,
sunken eyes with small pale pupils, a lipless grin showing the teeth, dark
rotted patches on the arms and legs, a torn and ragged blue sleeveless
basketball jersey with a yellow number 13, torn blue shorts with white and
yellow trim, white high-top sneakers with blue and yellow flashes over white
socks. Identical colours, identical proportions, identical build and identical
height as the reference, in every frame.

LAYOUT: one horizontal row of 4 frames of equal width, evenly spaced. No
borders, no frame numbers, no labels, no background, no drop shadows.

POSE GUIDE: TWO images are attached, and they do different jobs.

The COLOUR image of the character is the only authority on WHO HE IS. His
colours, his proportions, his build, his height, his face, his kit and the
drawing style all come from that image and from the SUBJECT above, and nothing
below changes any of them. It does NOT decide which way he faces: in that
drawing he is turned toward the right edge, and in this sheet he is not.

The other image is a POSE GUIDE: a plain black stick figure on a white
background, four figures standing in a row on one ground line, in the same
left-to-right order as the FRAMES listed below. The Nth figure in the pose
guide is the pose for the Nth frame. Take the GEOMETRY from it and only the
geometry: where each foot stands on the ground line, how deeply the knees are
bent, how far down his shoulders and head have come, and where BOTH hands are.
Where the words below and the pose guide describe the same thing, they agree;
the pose guide is the exact version of it.

THE BODY ON THE POSE GUIDE is seen from the front while he bends forward TOWARD
THE VIEWER. That is why, in the second and third figures, the shoulders sit so
close above the hips: the chest is tipped toward the camera, not squashed. Draw
a man bending forward at the waist and the knees, seen from the front.

THE HANDS ON THE POSE GUIDE are the narrow shapes at the end of each arm. BOTH
hands do the same thing in every frame, one on each side of his centre line,
the same height as each other: this is a two-handed move.

THE HEAD ON THE POSE GUIDE: the small TRIANGLE in the middle of the face is his
nose, and the two small ovals on either side of the head are BOTH of his ears.
His face points toward the viewer in every frame: nose in the middle of his
face, both ears showing equally. The upright line down the face marks its
centre and the level line his eyes. The short lines on top are his hair, at
rest.

Draw the character from the colour reference standing in those positions. The
pose guide is an instruction, not artwork: its thin flat lines, its joint dots,
its white background, its circular head, its triangle, its ovals and its face
lines are NOT part of the drawing and must not appear anywhere in it.

CAMERA: locked off. Identical distance and eye level in every frame. The
character must be exactly the same height in every frame, and the same height
as in the reference image — do not zoom, crop, recompose or rescale between
frames. All frames share one ground line: the soles of the feet touch the same
horizontal line in every frame.

VIEW: front view, facing the viewer, squared to camera: his chest, his hips and
his face all point out of the picture, both shoulders the same distance from
the camera, the number on his jersey in the middle of his chest. In frames 2, 3
and 4 his feet are planted a little wider than his shoulders, and they stay
exactly where they are: he bends, he does not step.

CRITICAL: this is a TWO-HANDED move, and it is SYMMETRICAL. In every frame both
hands are at the same height, one each side of his centre line, doing the same
thing. Neither hand dribbles.

THE BALL IS NOT DRAWN, but it is there: the game draws a basketball on the
floor between his feet in frames 2 and 3, and between his hands in frame 4. His
hands go where that ball is. In frames 3 and 4 there is a gap between his two
hands exactly as wide as a basketball -- about the width of his own head -- and
in that gap there is NOTHING: no ball, no shape, only empty background.

FRAMES, left to right:
1. CALIBRATION POSE: standing straight upright, feet shoulder-width apart, arms
   hanging relaxed at his sides, facing the viewer, in the plain neutral
   standing pose from the reference image. This exact pose appears as the first
   frame of every sheet in this set and must be drawn identically every time.
2. REACHING: bending forward at the waist, knees bending, both arms reaching
   straight down toward the floor in front of his feet, hands open, at the
   height of his shins. Head tipped forward, eyes on the floor in front of him.
3. SCOOPING, the lowest point: knees deeply bent and chest tipped well forward
   over his thighs, both hands down at the floor between his feet with the
   palms facing each other, fingers curled, cupping the two sides of a
   ball-sized gap. Head down, looking at the floor between his hands.
4. GATHERED: back up in his low athletic crouch, head up, looking at the
   viewer. Both forearms forward, both hands in front of his waistband with the
   palms facing each other, a ball-sized gap between them, as if holding a
   basketball in front of his belly with both hands.

This is a one-shot, not a loop. Frame 2 must continue naturally from a low
athletic standing stance, and frame 4 must settle back into that same stance.

STYLE: VGA-era 256-colour DOS-game pixel art, drawn pixel by pixel — NOT a
modern illustration with a pixel filter over it. The limits below are the look;
keep all of them: - At most THREE tones per material: a base, one darker
shadow, one lighter highlight. Hard edges between the tones. - NO gradients, NO
soft or airbrushed shading, NO glow, NO bloom, and NO anti-aliasing anywhere —
not on the outline, not between tones, not around the silhouette. - Where a
tone change needs softening, use visible ORDERED DITHER — a checkerboard of the
two tones. Dither, never blend. - Chunky square pixels on one consistent grid,
plainly visible at full size. - A bold dark outline around the silhouette and
around the major forms inside it. The background must be fully transparent
(alpha 0) with no haze, glow or soft fringe around the silhouette. Output a
wide landscape image.

The character is NOT holding a basketball in any frame, and none is drawn
anywhere: the game draws the ball separately, in the gap between his hands.
